items.explanation: School. に marks where you go.

example.reading: こどもは がっこうに いく。

items.explanation: House, home. 家 is also read うち, which means home and even 'my family'; 家に帰る is often read うちに かえる.
items.culture_note: People take their shoes off at the entrance (玄関, げんかん) before stepping into a home.

items.mnemonic: Eki: 'Eek, I missed the train at the station!'

example.reading: えきは どこですか。

items.explanation: Shop, store. Staff greet customers with いらっしゃいませ (welcome).
items.mnemonic: Mise: 'Me, say, what does this shop sell?'

example.reading: この みせは やすい。

items.explanation: Hospital. Careful: 美容院 (びよういん, hair salon) differs only in the length of よ.
items.mnemonic: Byō-in: being ill (病) puts you in a hospital.

example.reading: ちちは びょういんに いる。
example.meaning: My father is at the hospital.

items.explanation: Bank. 銀 means silver. で marks where an action happens; 働く (はたらく) means to work.
items.mnemonic: Gin-kō: silver coins go into the bank.

example.reading: あねは ぎんこうで はたらく。
example.meaning: My older sister works at a bank.

items.explanation: Company, and by extension the office where you work.

example.reading: ちちは かいしゃに いく。
example.meaning: My father goes to the office.

items.explanation: Toilet, from English. お手洗い (おてあらい) is more polite. あそこ means over there.

example.reading: トイレは あそこだ。

items.culture_note: Toilets with heated seats and built-in bidet functions are common in Japanese homes.

items.explanation: Room. Its reading is special: it belongs to the whole word, not to each kanji.
items.mnemonic: Heya: 'Hey ya, come into my room!'

example.reading: わたしの へやは ちいさい。

items.explanation: Country. The question literally asks 'where is your country?'
items.mnemonic: Kuni: 'Cool, need a passport for this country.'

example.word: あなたの国はどこですか。
example.reading: あなたの くには どこですか。
